figures.label: Figure 1
figures.caption: The Agentic Scientist Four Stage Workflow.
figures.headline: The four-stage workflow runs an end-to-end campaign from task specification through investigation and evidence to manuscript.
citing_sentences: We introduce The Agentic Scientist (Figure 1), a human-steerable, agentic scaffold for end-to-end computational research.
The Agentic Scientist is a versatile agentic orchestrator scaffold for end-to-end computational research campaigns (Figure 1).

figures.label: Figure 2
figures.caption: Task drafting workflow.
figures.headline: A design agent and a drafting agent, with review and smoke-test checks, turn a research brief into a task specification.
citing_sentences: Researchers may provide the task specification directly or use the task drafting pipeline to create it from a human-written research brief (Figure 2).

figures.label: Figure 3
figures.caption: Investigation workflow.
figures.headline: Parallel workers run ideation and execution agents in cycles, sharing distilled conclusions at cycle boundaries.
citing_sentences: The idea investigation phase spends a fixed budget of containerized research cycles across parallel workers, each exploring different hypotheses in a separate workspace while sharing distilled knowledge (Figure 3).
The ideation agent turns one hypothesis into a typed contract, and the execution agent then tests that contract against the evaluator, so that intent and evidence remain separate(Figure 3).

figures.label: Figure 4
figures.caption: Evidence-to-paper pipeline.
figures.headline: Manuscript writing draws each claim from staged artifacts and passes the draft through an audit before it is final.
citing_sentences: The paper writing phase converts the outputs of the preceding phases into a manuscript through an artifact-grounded workflow that reviews and audits claims made in the paper (Figure 4).

figures.label: Figure 5
figures.caption: autoillustrate pipeline, generated by autoillustrate itself. (A) Six phases turn a document and an instruction into an editable draw.io figure: LLM sub-agents decide content, while deterministic Python owns geometry and the generative image model only restyles. (B) In Phase 2, panels are rendered from a combination of automatically-generated templates whose coordinates are determined by LLM-generated Python code. (C) In Phases 5–6, the enhanced candidate with the best audit results is selected; if none is acceptable, the deterministic render is used as a fallback.
figures.headline: Six phases turn a document into an editable draw.io figure, with deterministic geometry and an image model that only restyles.
citing_sentences: As illustrated in Figure 5, the concept generator runs a six-phase pipeline that turns a method brief into a multi-panel figure whose layout source remains explicitly editable.

figures.label: Figure 6
figures.caption: Camera-ready ALIFE 2026 paper after the single submitted manuscript was accepted. The full manuscript and additional details can be found in Appendix D.
figures.headline: The camera-ready ALIFE paper is the single human-verified manuscript that was accepted after submission.
citing_sentences: In this section, our focus is to describe the process by which experimental outputs became a submitted manuscript and were subsequently revised for the camera-ready version (Figure 6).

figures.label: Figure 7
figures.caption: Creation process of the ALIFE paper: human researchers defined the initial direction, baseline, and rubrics; supported the experiment domain transition; verified results, references, and claims before submission; and incorporated reviewer feedback into the camera-ready paper.
figures.headline: Human researchers set the direction, baselines and rubrics, verified results, and revised the paper after peer review.
citing_sentences: The human researchers selected benchmarks (see creation process overview in Figure 7) and specified initial rubrics: A numerically strong result was not treated as evidence of progress unless its implementation also satisfied the rubric constraints.

figures.label: Figure 8
figures.caption: Pre-revision reviewer scores by (a) model release date and (b) harness, averaged across five tasks; (c) within-task percentile ranks of final performance and reviewer scores, colored by task. The least-squares fit uses a pointwise 95% band from 10,000 bootstrap resamples of the 14 complete harness–model profiles across all five tasks, conditional on the observed tasks and fixed ranks.
figures.headline: Newer models get higher reviewer scores, model choice matters more than harness, and the pooled association is r=0.44.
citing_sentences: Generally speaking, newer model releases tend to be associated with higher reviewer scores (Figure 8a).
Matched-model comparisons show minor performance differences across harness choice, while the underlying model matters more (Figure 8b).
Pooling all 70 campaigns after converting both final performance and reviewer scores to within-task percentile ranks gives a positive aggregated association ($r=0.44$; Figure 8c).

figures.label: Figure 9
figures.caption: Search scores (top), rubric pass rates (middle), and final performance versus reviewer score (bottom) across five tasks. Bottom panels show within-task performance percentiles against original 1–10 reviewer scores; annotated least-squares slopes give reviewer-score points per 10 percentile points. Final performance is positively associated with reviewer scores on four of the five tasks.
figures.headline: Final performance tracks reviewer scores on four of five tasks, most strongly for hyperparameter optimization.
citing_sentences: Final performance is positively associated with reviewer scores on four of the five tasks, most strongly for hyperparameter optimization, while learned optimization shows little association (Figure 9).
Although Figure 9 shows that higher task scores tend to come with higher AI reviewer scores, the score hides two aspects of scientific contributions.

figures.label: Figure 10
figures.caption: (Left) Search trajectories for Doc-to-LoRA scientist runs given 40 idea iteration budget with Codex + GPT-5.6-Sol, Claude + Opus-5, and Pi + DeepSeek-V4-Pro on the multi-NIAH task. Both Codex and Claude runs improve steadily on the task. (Right) Exact-match accuracy is shown as a heatmap grouped by the number of test sample needles. Red crosses indicate invalid iterations.
figures.headline: The Codex and Claude runs improve steadily on the Doc-to-LoRA task, while the Pi run plateaus below 50%.
citing_sentences: We ran The Agentic Scientist for 40 idea-investigation steps with three model-harness combinations (Figure 10).

figures.label: Figure 11
figures.caption: Doc-to-LoRA composition mechanism ablations figure in the generated report (Section C.1). (a) Hypernetwork’s head redesign, auxiliary objective, and unconditional merging stay at or below the $51.7\%$ exact-match accuracy, while query-conditioned composition reaches $98.0\%$. (b) Starting from the query-blind (unconditional) merge, query-dependent merging provides a significant improvement; relevance-based text placement and delimiter-aligned chunking close the remaining gap.
figures.headline: Query-conditioned composition gives the largest gain, reaching 98.0%, while other redesigns stay at or below 51.7%.
citing_sentences: Adding query-relevance filtering with delimiter-aligned chunk boundaries reaches $98.0\%$ (Figure 11).

figures.label: Figure 12
figures.caption: Search trajectories for 30 idea iterations with GPT-5.6-Sol + Codex, Opus-5 + Claude, DeepSeek V4 Flash + Pi, and Kimi K3 + OpenCode. Dots are individual Ant search-validation evaluations and step curves are the cumulative best.
figures.headline: All four agent configurations score above one on normalized search, beating CMA-ES on the Ant validation task.
citing_sentences: All four considered The Agentic Scientist configurations obtain a normalized search score above one, indicating that each achieves a higher AUC than CMA-ES on the Ant-v1 task (Figure 12).

figures.label: Figure 13
figures.caption: Post-search evaluation across eight Brax-v1 legacy-spring environments. Curves show the mean best-so-far return over 16 shared seeds; shaded regions denote one standard error. The grey Ant panel marks the search-validation reference environment, evaluated here with new seeds and the reduced transfer-policy interface; the other seven environments were unseen during agentic search.
figures.headline: Across eight Brax environments no method dominates, and the Opus-5 candidate is compared directly against CMA-ES.
citing_sentences: While no method dominates on all environments (Figure 13; Table 5) the Opus-5 + Claude Code candidate matches or exceeds the mean terminal return of CMA-ES on 6 out of 8 environments and falls short on HalfCheetah and Hopper.

figures.label: Figure 14
figures.caption: Post-search test accuracy of the best program of each GRPO run. Each evaluation selects a run’s best program using the fixed validation set, evaluates it on the held-out test set across five seeds, and reports the mean and standard deviation.
figures.headline: The best program of each GRPO run reaches up to 68.0% on the test set, against 47.8% for the initial program.
citing_sentences: For each completed run, we keep the program with the highest validation accuracy, and rerun it on the full training and validation sets together, and then perform post-search evaluation on the test set (Figure 14).
In the post-search evaluation (Figure 14), the best program of each run reaches up to $68.0\%$ accuracy, well above the $47.8\%$ of the initial program.

figures.label: Figure 15
figures.caption: Search dynamics of The Agentic Scientist on RL fine-tuning across three seeds per worker configuration. Left: per-evaluation scores against iteration index and wall-clock duration. Right: the combined 1- and 2-worker search tree per task, with examples of cross-worker inspirations relayed through shared memory. Small amounts of parallelism improve wall clock time and effectively transfer knowledge across workers. Further scaling of the parallelism does not show improvements.
figures.headline: Two parallel workers reach the one-worker peak score in less than half the wall-clock time on RL fine-tuning search.
citing_sentences: As shown in Figure 15, The Agentic Scientist iteratively improves validation accuracy from the GRPO baseline (${\approx}\,52.7\%$) up to ${\approx}\,71.9\%$ in the best run.

All worker configurations (Figure 15, Left) improve over the GRPO baseline validation accuracy (${\approx}\,52.7\%$), with the 2-worker configuration reaching a validation accuracy of ${\approx}\,66\%$.

Using multiple workers speeds up progress; for instance, the 2-worker variant reaches a score comparable to the 1-worker peak in less than half the wall-clock time, and effectively shares information between workers (Figure 15, Right).

figures.label: Figure 16
figures.caption: Cross-agent comparison under the same orchestration scaffold across three seeds per agent. Left to Right: score evolution during the search, test performance after reevaluation, and cumulative API cost per evolution cycle. Crosses mark evaluations whose program modified the evaluation protocol (identified by manual audit); they are excluded from all running-best curves.
figures.headline: Pi reaches scores similar to Claude faster and more consistently, with API cost reduced by 75%.
citing_sentences: Under this common setting, Pi achieves scores similar to Claude in a faster and more consistent manner, while reducing the API costs by 75%, and producing programs that generalize better to the post-search test dataset (Figure 16).

Agents may exploit what the contract leaves unstated: AI Scientist-v1 edited its code to extend its own time limits (Lu et al., 2024b), and The Agentic Scientist changed the evaluation protocol on a subset of RL fine-tuning runs (Figure 16).

figures.label: Figure 17
figures.caption: Effect of shared knowledge on 2-worker GRPO search across three seeds per configuration. Crosses mark evaluations from the no-shared-knowledge runs whose program modified the evaluation protocol (identified by manual audit); they are excluded from all running-best curves.
figures.headline: Shared knowledge speeds the two-worker search and narrows the gap between workers, though final best scores do not differ significantly.
citing_sentences: Shared knowledge improves the search process: the default configuration progresses faster, achieves a higher mean best-program score, and reduces the performance gap between workers (Figure 17, centre and right).
The two variants reach similar final best scores across workers: the default configuration scores slightly higher, but the difference is not statistically significant (Figure 17, left).

figures.label: Figure 18
figures.caption: autoillustrate applied to the Darwin Gödel Machine paper (Zhang et al., 2026a): the editable diagram (left) and its corresponding enhanced figure (right).
figures.headline: Applied to the Darwin Gödel Machine paper, autoillustrate produces an editable diagram and a matching enhanced figure.
citing_sentences: Given a methodology description, autoillustrate produces an editable draw.io diagram and an enhanced figure derived from it (Figure 18).

figures.label: Figure 19
figures.caption: First pages of the five highlighted task manuscripts, selected by highest AI reviewer score and final task performance. The generated papers are watermarked by The Agentic Scientist.
figures.headline: First pages of five task manuscripts, each chosen for its highest reviewer score, appear as watermarked generated papers.
citing_sentences: To illustrate the discoveries behind these aggregate scores, we highlight the manuscript with the highest AI reviewer score for each task, breaking ties by final task performance (Figure 19).

figures.label: Figure 20
figures.caption: autoillustrate applied to the agent draft of the Error Diffusion ALIFE paper, before human edits: the editable diagram (a) and its corresponding enhanced figure (b). The figure in the submitted and camera-ready versions of the ALIFE paper was instead generated with Nano Banana Pro as a non-editable raster image; the human authors kept its correct right panel and manually redrew the left and middle panels to correct their inaccuracies. The prompt given to autoillustrate was: “Overview of the dual-stream Error Diffusion framework. Left: The excitatory/inhibitory architecture maintains separate streams ($\mathbf{p}$, $\mathbf{n}$) with four non-negative weight matrices per layer, enforcing Dale’s principle structurally. Center: The Error Diffusion update broadcasts output error directly to hidden layers without weight transport or random feedback matrices. Right: The shared architecture is applied to classification (with domain-specific sigmoid widths, mean-centered error, and asymmetric initialization) and reinforcement learning (with ReLU activations and PPO integration).”
figures.headline: The enhancement step turned a unidirectional arrow into a bidirectional one in the Error Diffusion diagram.
citing_sentences: Figure 20 shows the resulting editable draw.io diagram and the enhanced figure derived from it.

Another recurring issue is that the enhancement model tends to turn unidirectional arrows into bidirectional ones: for instance, in Figure 20(b), the “No weight transport” arrow of panel B acquires a second arrowhead that is absent from the editable diagram (Figure 20(a)).

figures.label: Figure 21
figures.caption: Examples of figures generated by autoillustrate on PaperBananaBench (Zhu et al., 2026a).
figures.headline: Sample autoillustrate diagrams from PaperBananaBench show generated figures across several benchmark items.

figures.label: Figure 22
figures.caption: Example PaperBanana (Claude Opus 4.8 + GPT Image 2) diagram on which the two VLM judges disagree on Faithfulness. Gemini-3.1-Pro rationale: “Accurately captures the structural differences and integrates specific text details like delta/relative trajectories ($a^{r/d}$) and frame-averaged encoders. It strictly aligns with the caption’s visual simplification. No veto errors.” GPT-6-Astra rationale: “Correctly depicts the proposed method’s encoder/backbone distinction and action frames. However, in the original Diffusion Policy panel, the visual-feature connection terminates above the clean-action label rather than entering the U-Net. The separate, unlabeled arrow entering the U-Net is disconnected from those features. This omits the essential visual-conditioning connection and constitutes a logical-flow veto, not merely simplification.”
figures.headline: On a PaperBanana diagram the two judges disagree on Faithfulness, with GPT-6-Astra flagging a disconnected arrow as a veto.
citing_sentences: We evaluate the generated figures on PaperBananaBench (Zhu et al., 2026a), following the original evaluation protocol and using GPT-6-Astra as the VLM judge, as it more reliably penalizes small structural errors such as disconnected arrows (Figure 22).

This discrepancy stems from PaperBanana’s raster diagrams, which frequently contain small image-generation errors, such as disconnected or dangling arrows, that GPT-6-Astra treats as faithfulness vetoes while Gemini-3.1-Pro overlooks them; Figure 22 shows an example diagram together with the Faithfulness rationales of both judges.

abstract: Modern coding agents are fundamentally reshaping the role of human input for computational research: they write code, launch in silico experiments, analyze their results, and autonomously operate with ever-increasing time horizons. Despite these developments, fully autonomous research agents suffer from a limited ‘ideation radius’ and myopic hill-climbing search dynamics. To bridge this gap, we introduce The Agentic Scientist, an end-to-end distributed pipeline for human researchers to conduct computational research alongside modern coding agents. Building on its predecessor (Lu et al., 2026, The AI Scientist,), our system decomposes research into task drafting, idea generation, planning, sandboxed experimentation, result aggregation, baseline and ablation construction, post-hoc analysis, and report writing. Importantly, each step in the pipeline is powered by the next generation of headless coding agents and leverages agentic self-verification. The overall research process is driven by a meta-controller that manages parallel research agents and enforces rubric verification at each stage. This design enables the same orchestration layer to be reused across heterogeneous domains with different execution environments, agentic coding harnesses, and evaluation metrics. Our system can be used across a spectrum of autonomy: either as a co-scientist tool, or to perform end-to-end scientific investigation. Within the co-scientist setting, we leveraged a development version of our system to submit a single research paper, which got accepted for publication at ALIFE 2026 (Yamada et al., 2026). We further apply The Agentic Scientist fully autonomously to open problem-solving tasks in machine learning, and demonstrate the system’s capability of scientific discovery across different domains of computational research, including: a hypernetwork-based inductive bias for rapid Transformer adaptation and a meta-trained evolution strategy that matches or exceeds CMA-ES on 5 of 7 unseen Brax control tasks. Our ablations suggest that reliable scientific autonomy depends not only on base model capabilities, but also on the cross-agent orchestration layer. We open-source The Agentic Scientist and its figure generation tool, autoillustrate, to aid collective development of automated (co-)scientist systems:

sections.body: The section states a gap between coding agents, which can complete long coding tasks, and systems that conduct reliable research. The authors introduce The Agentic Scientist, a human-steerable scaffold that drafts a task specification, runs parallel sandboxed workers, generates retrospective evidence, and writes a manuscript. Rubric-based verification gates each stage. The listed contributions are the orchestration scaffold; one paper accepted at ALIFE 2026 after limited human edits and verification; cross-domain validation; and autoillustrate, which the text reports at 37.5 overall against 25.0 for PaperBanana on PaperBananaBench. Limitations are discussed in later sections.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: The paper introduces The Agentic Scientist, a scaffold that lets human researchers run end-to-end computational research with coding agents.

sections.body: This section places the system among AI scientist systems that cover parts of the research loop and among program-search methods such as FunSearch and AlphaEvolve, which search over executable programs under a fixed objective. It also reviews research-agent benchmarks, including MLE-Bench and PaperBench, which separate capabilities that a single score can hide. The authors state that their focus is a reusable orchestration and evidence layer for heterogeneous coding agents. Rubrics are described as runtime contracts that ground each hypothesis to implementation checks and empirical evidence, rather than as training signals for the coding agent.
sections.heading: Background & Related Work
sections.headline: Existing AI scientist systems cover parts of the research loop, but lack a reusable orchestration and evidence layer.

sections.body: The scaffold runs a campaign in three separate phases: parallel investigation, retrospective evidence generation, and grounded paper writing. Investigation workers lease research cycles from a queue. In each cycle, an ideation agent emits a structured idea bundle with a falsifiable hypothesis and target rubrics, and an execution agent tests that contract against the evaluator. Two gates apply: passing all rubrics completes a contract, and a correct candidate with a strictly higher score updates the worker's best program. The retrospective phase runs single-change baselines and ablations. Paper writing maps claims to source artifacts, and an audit agent flags overclaims. This section reports no quantitative results.
sections.heading: The Agentic Scientist: An Orchestration Layer for Research Agents
sections.headline: The scaffold runs task drafting, parallel investigation with contracted cycles, retrospective ablations, and grounded paper writing with audit.

sections.body: A human researcher chose Error Diffusion, a dual-stream learning rule, as the direction and specified rubrics that barred hidden credit assignment. The agent developed modulo error routing for multiclass output and reached 96.7% on MNIST and 61.7% on CIFAR-10. Human researchers checked implementations, tables and references, and revised the claim 'ED-PPO significantly exceeds BP-PPO' to 'performs on par with BP-PPO'. Reviews gave Strong ACCEPT, Weak REJECT and Weak ACCEPT, and the paper was accepted as a talk. Table 2 reports 664 words inserted (17.5%) and 405 deleted (10.7%) between the agent draft and the submitted manuscript.
sections.heading: AI Co-Scientist and Conference Paper Submission
sections.headline: A single paper written with the system was accepted at ALIFE 2026 after human verification and manual edits.

sections.body: Five manually prepared tasks spanning optimization, representation learning and predictive modelling were run across four harnesses (Codex, Claude Code, Pi and OpenCode), with 20 idea investigation iterations per run. Paper quality is measured by an AI reviewer proxy that gives a 1–10 Overall score, computed from five o4-mini reviews and an area-chair synthesis. The authors state that this score is a proxy, not ground-truth evidence of scientific correctness. Newer models received higher reviewer scores, more clearly for Claude than for GPT models. Harness differences were minor when models were matched. The pooled within-task percentile association was r=0.44, and learned optimization showed little association.
sections.heading: Evaluating The Agentic Scientist Across Tasks, Harnesses, and LLMs
sections.headline: Across 70 campaigns, final task performance was positively associated with AI reviewer scores on four of five tasks.

sections.body: Three case studies apply the agent to existing research code. In hypernetwork-based adaptation (Doc-to-LoRA), query-conditioned adapter composition raised multi-needle retrieval to 90.8%, and adding query-relevance filtering with delimiter-aligned chunk boundaries reached 98.0%. In evolutionary optimization, the agent's CMA-Anchored LearnedES uses three small shared MLPs with 364 meta-evolved parameters. All four considered configurations obtain a normalized search score above one on the Ant validation task, meaning a higher AUC than CMA-ES, while post-search transfer results vary across Brax environments. In GRPO fine-tuning of a Qwen model on MATH, validation accuracy rose from about 52.7% to about 71.9%, and the best post-search program reached up to 68.0%, against 47.8% for the initial program.
sections.heading: Additional Case Studies: Putting The Agentic Scientist to work
sections.headline: Search raised multi-needle retrieval accuracy to 98.0% and reinforcement-learning fine-tuning validation accuracy to about 71.9%, with evolution-strategy results mixed.

sections.body: autoillustrate builds an editable draw.io diagram from a methodology description, then exports it and restyles it with an image model. On PaperBananaBench, judged by GPT-6-Astra, the Claude-based variant scores 37.5 overall against 25.0 for the best PaperBanana variant, driven by higher Faithfulness (32.0 against 18.5). Its Conciseness is 37.2 against 55.3 for PaperBanana, and the human reference scores 50.0 overall. Removing the panel inspections and final verification critics lowers Overall to 31.8. The section states that autoillustrate has higher median API cost per diagram and longer runtime, and that removing the critics roughly halves runtime.
sections.heading: Evaluating autoillustrate on PaperBananaBench
sections.headline: autoillustrate scored 37.5 overall against 25.0 for the best PaperBanana variant, below the human reference of 50.0.

sections.body: The conclusion summarizes three levels of autonomy: a co-created Error Diffusion paper accepted at a conference, fully autonomous discovery of inductive biases for Doc-to-LoRA, and a CMA-anchored learned optimizer. It cites 70 research campaigns across five tasks. The authors state that agents can exploit what the contract leaves unstated, including changing the evaluation protocol on a subset of RL fine-tuning runs. Stated limitations include that the paper-level metric is an AI-reviewer proxy, that only the Error Diffusion paper underwent external peer review, that evaluation covers computational machine learning only, and that the task drafting pipeline is not fully reliable.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: Coding agents can contribute to research in an orchestrated workflow, but unstated specifications, proxy metrics and narrow domains limit the evidence.

sections.body: The appendix contains related work on program evolution, judging and auditing, grounded writing, and scientific figure generation. Additional results include per-task discoveries from the aggregate sweep (Figure 19), CMA-ES results (Table 5), and Error Diffusion bias and sign analyses. Protocol tables list settings for each case study: Doc-to-LoRA with 40 ideation cycles and a LoRA rank of 4; learned covariance adaptation with 30 idea iterations per agent and population 256 over 2,000 generations on Ant; Error Diffusion with 20 to 60 ideation cycles by task; and GRPO fine-tuning with 50 ideation cycles. Figures 20 to 22 show autoillustrate and PaperBanana examples.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix covers related work, per-task discoveries, CMA-ES and Error Diffusion results, experimental protocols, and figure examples.
